craft_claim: Sound-meaning correspondences (iconicity) are statistically real across languages, so phonetic texture can reinforce sense when sound and meaning are deliberately aligned.

supporting_evidence.location: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 113(39):10818-10823
supporting_evidence.note: Blasi and colleagues found statistically significant non-arbitrary sound-meaning associations across roughly two-thirds of the sampled languages, establishing iconicity as a real cross-linguistic tendency.
Perniss, Thompson and Vigliocco review evidence from spoken and signed languages that iconicity is a general property of language rather than a marginal curiosity.

counterevidence.note: Iconicity is graded and language-specific; the arbitrary sign remains dominant, so sound-sense alignment cannot be assumed and does not guarantee emotional effect.

scope: Short, sound-sensitive passages in any form where the phonetics can be chosen to match the sense.
exceptions: Translation, where the source-language sound-symbolism is usually lost.
Technical vocabulary with no sensory analogue.
